name: Request Denied
summary: Understand LinkedIn 999 Request Denied: anti-scraping detection, automated request blocking, and bypass prevention.
explanation:
Automated or scraping traffic detected by LinkedIn
receives the 999 Request Denied status code.
The code falls outside the valid
100 to 599 range and is not registered with
IANA. The number is the highest possible three-digit
integer.
Table of ContentsUsageExampleThe reason phrase is emptyHow to fixSee also
Usage
LinkedIn returns 999 Request Denied when its
security infrastructure determines a request is not
from a legitimate browser session. The evaluation
runs at the platform edge before the request reaches
the application layer.
Triggers include:

User agent filtering. Requests with non-browser
user agents (curl, python-requests, wget,
custom scrapers) are blocked. The same URL accessed
through a standard web browser returns
200 OK.
Rate limiting. An abnormally high number of
requests from the same IP address or network within
a short window triggers the block.
IP reputation. Requests from IP addresses
associated with prior abuse, data center ranges,
or cloud hosting providers are more likely to
receive a 999.
robots.txt violations. Crawlers ignoring
LinkedIn's robots.txt restrictions encounter
999 responses.

The block is automatic and temporary. LinkedIn
states access is restored once network activity
returns to normal. Connecting through a different
network during the block period bypasses the
restriction.

Note
The HTTP specification defines valid status
codes as three-digit integers between 100
and 599, and notes implementations often use
values from 600 to 999 for internal
communication of non-HTTP conditions. A client
receiving a response with an invalid status
code processes the response as a
5xx server error.

SEO impact
Google's status code documentation covers the
1xx through 5xx classes only, leaving 999
outside the defined behavior. Crawlers are
likely to treat a 999 response as an error,
reduce crawl frequency, and eventually drop
persistently affected URLs from the index.

Example
A command-line tool sends a GET request to a
LinkedIn profile page. Visited in a web browser,
the URL returns the profile of
Fili (the creator of this
website). Using curl, LinkedIn returns 999.
curl Command
curl -sS -o /dev/null -D- https://www.linkedin.com/in/filiwiese

Request
GET /in/filiwiese HTTP/1.1
Host: www.linkedin.com
User-Agent: curl/8.5.0
Accept: */*

Response
HTTP/2 999
content-type: text/html
content-length: 1530
pragma: no-cache
cache-control: no-cache, no-store, no-transform
strict-transport-security: max-age=31536000
x-content-type-options: nosniff

The same URL accessed through a standard web browser
with a full browser user agent string returns
200 OK.
The reason phrase is empty
Reference material universally names the code "999
Request Denied", and LinkedIn sends no reason
phrase at all. Requesting over HTTP/1.1 returns a
status line carrying the number followed by nothing,
which curl renders as <none>.
HTTP/1.1 999 <none>

The HTTP/2 responses shown above carry no reason
phrase either, since the protocol dropped the field
entirely. "Request Denied" is therefore a convention
of documentation rather than anything the server
transmits, and tooling parsing the phrase finds an
empty string.
No Retry-After header accompanies the
response, so a client has no stated interval to wait
before trying again.
How to fix
The 999 response targets automated access patterns.
Strategies depend on whether the access is legitimate.
For monitoring tools and uptime checkers: Configure
the tool to use a realistic browser
User-Agent string. Reduce check
frequency to avoid triggering rate limits. Use
LinkedIn's official API endpoints with proper
Authentication instead of scraping public pages.
For link checkers and validators: Exclude
LinkedIn URLs from automated validation. The 999
response does not indicate a broken link. The page
is accessible through a browser. Tools like
html-proofer and site validators commonly encounter
this false positive.
For legitimate API access: Use the
LinkedIn API
with OAuth 2.0 Authentication. Authenticated API
requests return standard HTTP status codes and are not
subject to the 999 block.
If blocked from browser access: LinkedIn states
the block lifts automatically once network activity
returns to normal. Switching to a different network
connection bypasses the block immediately. If the
issue persists, contact LinkedIn support. The block
cannot be lifted manually, but support investigates
the triggering activity.
